source.title: Perspective: A Phase Diagram for Deep Learning unifying Jamming, Feature Learning and Lazy Training
source.authors: M. Geiger; Leonardo Petrini; M. Wyart

record.tranche_reason: The paper presents width sweeps and generalization results that bear on V2, using its own phase-diagram experiments and measures.
record.gate_note: The paper tests how test error changes with width, including individual-network and ensemble curves. Cited results from other work are not extracted as this paper's results. Its experiments use binary classification on reduced MNIST and CIFAR-10, not the full natural-label benchmarks in V1.
record.test_reason: The study supplies new width sweeps measuring held-out classification error beyond the zero-training-loss threshold, testing V2 in two-hidden-layer networks on reduced, PCA-projected binary image datasets.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the width results: individual-network error peaks near jamming and subsequently decreases with width, while ensemble averaging improves intermediate-width performance and removes double descent. The authors explain the second descent through diminishing initialization fluctuations and organize these findings within a phase diagram separating underparameterized, lazy-training, and feature-learning regimes.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses fully connected networks with two hidden layers and gradient descent on reduced binary datasets; it also compares individual and ensemble predictors.
record.method_sensitivity: The test-error curve and location of the jamming transition vary with dataset, initialization scale, and ensemble averaging. The text says ensemble averaging removes double descent.

fits_no_version.finding: Averaging 20 independently initialized predictors improves intermediate-width performance and removes double descent; ensemble error varies only weakly with width beyond jamming.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ensembling independently initialized networks can recover much of the generalization benefit of widening individual networks by reducing initialization-dependent fluctuations.

record.problems: The relevant curves are presented as figures without numeric values in the text. The experiments use reduced, projected, binary datasets and a specific fully connected architecture and gradient-descent procedure.

untested.parts: Paired random-label fitting and natural-label generalization experiments; random-label held-out accuracy.

The original one-hidden-layer architecture and full multiclass MNIST/downsampled CIFAR-10 settings are not tested; the new experiments use two hidden layers and reduced, PCA-projected binary datasets.
Direct convolutional versus fully connected comparisons and the contribution of local connectivity; relevant discussion reviews other studies.
Adaptive versus nonadaptive optimizer generalization under specified tuning budgets.
Batch-size effects under matched epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects and interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus removing random examples.

missing.what: Individual-network MNIST width sweeps at rescaled initialization amplitudes 10 and 10^6. R1 records only 0.004, omitting the additional initialization regimes supporting the width result.
missing.locator: Section 1.4 and Figure 5, left panel; Section 3

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source listed for V2. No limits_scope verdict follows merely from the interpolation peak, different experimental setting, or ensemble improvement. Figures 7–10 largely reproduce attributed earlier results and should not be added as new experiments of this study.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label test performance in the same networks.

The experiments use fully connected networks with two hidden layers, gradient descent, binary classification, and reduced MNIST/CIFAR-10 data; they do not test one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on the specified MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10 settings.
No direct comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks' test errors or of local connectivity.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurement or comparison against norm- and margin-based measures.
